The State Department says it's moving some diplomats
out of the Middle East amid new concerns
about possible attacks from Iran
and ongoing threats from the Houthis in Yemen.
NPR's Michelle Kellerman reports
most U.S. embassies in the region
have been operating with limited staff.
The Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton,
says the administration has received information
that Iran has "substantially increased efforts
to target U.S. personnel."
He tells Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a memo
that the plots have reached advanced stages
in both the Middle East and certain other countries.
The State Department confirmed the unclassified memo
and said that the new intelligence
is informing staffing adjustments at its embassies.
Earlier this week, some diplomats and family members
were evacuated from the U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia
because of attacks from Yemen.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News.
More than 70,000 police officers
have been deployed across France today
amid ongoing demonstrations,
overschool staffing shortages, and the cost of living.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports several cities,
including parts of Paris, have issued curfews for minors.
Many Paris shopkeepers still reeling
from the destruction and violence of last weekend
have boarded up their stores.
In Lyon, Nice and Montpellier,
marches have been banned for security reasons.
In Paris, authorities have diverted some protest routes
away from shopping streets and public buildings
to limit possible damage.
President Emmanuel Macron, who has been criticized
for being absent from the crisis,
met with high school students for the first time
to hear their grievances.
He said the government would work with them to find solutions.
But critics say he has already lost French youth.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
Stocks on Wall Street ended the week
mixed with the Dow Jones Industrial Average
posting a slight gain despite a sharp drop on Friday.
The NASDAQ and S&P both lost ground for the week.
NPR's Ravi El-Nam reports concerns about rising oil prices
and artificial intelligence dominated trading.
The real action this week took place in the second half
when surging crude prices and intentions in the Middle East
sparked renewed fears about inflation
and the broader economy.
Rising energy costs have been a big drag on markets
ever since the war with Iran started earlier this year.
And then concerns about AI also resurfaced.
Meta said it would need to continue spending
massive amounts of money on AI,
hammering stocks across the sector.
For investors, the main concern is whether all this borrowing
being done to pursue AI dominance can be sustained,
especially as interest rates are rising.
Rafael Nam, NPR News.
This is NPR.
Severe flooding in the Four Corners region of the US
has led to water rescues and left some roads impassable.
Crews in New Mexico and Colorado
are using National Guard boats and helicopters
to reach stranded residents.
Some people have been told to evacuate
while others are being urged to stay put
until water levels drop.
The governor of Colorado has declared
a disaster emergency for flooding
as Tropical Storm Trudy moves through the region.
Jamie Wonsack reports the conditions have forced
the temporary closure of a local river.
Local law enforcement has closed the Animas River
to kayaks, canoes, and other recreation
due to rapidly changing flood conditions.
Rob Farino is the Director of Emergency Management
in La Plata County.
We have a concern about high water, switch water rescues

The county doesn't want to spend resources
on a potential water rescue.
Emergency services are stretched thin,
responding to evacuations and road closures
across the region.
For NPR News, I'm Jamie Wonsack in Durango, Colorado.

The White House says the Department of Agriculture
will offer $5 billion in loan guarantees
to modernize meat and seafood processing.
The administration says a voluntary US-caught seafood label
will identify seafood harvested by American fishers.
